claims.claim: Only validated YAML front matter affects execution; Markdown prose and fenced code blocks remain inert.
limitations: The skill author remains trusted to define safe structured preconditions and postconditions.

claims.claim: An action labeled as external content is rejected before a side effect occurs.
limitations: Correct provenance labeling must be enforced by the integration that creates ActionRequest objects.

claims.claim: Command actions use argv arrays with shell=False and apply executable, argument, working-directory, and network policy checks.
limitations: An allowlisted interpreter or test suite can still perform behavior not visible from its executable name.

claims.claim: Command actions, preconditions, and postconditions use the declared expected exit-code set; undeclared codes, timeouts, signals, and failed assertions remain failures.

argv: command_action or command_timeout or signal_termination or postcondition_failure or expected_exit_codes

limitations: A declared exit code is an outcome contract, not proof of semantic correctness; postconditions and isolation remain required.
Portable declared process exits are restricted to integers from 0 through 255; signal return codes are never declarable.

claims.claim: File writes are relative, allowlisted, size-bounded, path-confined, and atomic.
limitations: The local snapshot backend does not provide an OS-level read-only filesystem outside the workspace.

claims.claim: A failed mutation restores the owned workspace snapshot and records a before/after tree hash.
limitations: Snapshot copying targets small local workspaces; copy-on-write and container backends remain separate concerns.

claims.claim: SQLite WAL persists runs, steps, approvals, events, and resume position while binding every idempotency key to one versioned canonical request and policy identity before replay.

argv: identity or idempot or resume or legacy or checkpoint_schema

limitations: SQLite is a single-node backend; distributed leases and fencing tokens are not implemented.
Canonical digests provide integrity binding, not authenticated identity.
Legacy rows without digest fields fail closed and cannot replay a result.

claims.claim: High-risk actions suspend until an unexpired, single-use approval bound to the exact canonical request, policy, and optional actor label is granted.
limitations: The local runtime has no external identity provider or cryptographic approver authentication.
A crash after approval consumption fails closed and requires a fresh approval before retry.

claims.claim: Outcome, rollback integrity, prompt-injection blocking, and attempt efficiency are scored from deterministic records.
limitations: Scores are task-specific rules, not a universal measure of agent quality.

claims.claim: Claims are expressed as strictly validated argv-only recipes with bounded time, output, paths, and default-deny networking.
limitations: A recipe describes bounded verification; it does not make untrusted code safe without a strong runtime backend.

claims.claim: The MCP server exposes evidence discovery by default and registers verification execution tools only after explicit user opt-in.
limitations: Remote deployment still requires transport authentication, origin validation, and deployment-specific hardening.

claims.claim: The OpenShell adapter uses a documented default-deny policy, argv-only invocation, automatic cleanup, and fails unsupported when the runtime is absent or not execution-ready.
limitations: CI validates adapter behavior and policy shape; a host with OpenShell is required to reproduce runtime isolation.
The readiness probe proves the reviewed version and an active gateway resolve for the launching session; it does not prove the sandbox enforces isolation, which remains issue #12.
OpenShell is an external runtime with its own documented maturity and threat model.

claims.claim: Docker and Podman adapters run a digestable verifier image with no network, a read-only source mount, a read-only root, dropped capabilities, quotas, and no-new-privileges.
limitations: Container isolation does not protect against container-runtime or host-kernel vulnerabilities.
External users should pin the verifier image by digest after a release is published.

claims.claim: Verification outputs can be packed into a deterministic archive with per-file SHA-256 integrity metadata.
limitations: SHA-256 proves integrity, not publisher identity; release attestations remain a separate supply-chain control.

claims.claim: MCP Registry metadata advertises read-only stdio distribution through PyPI and OCI packages with matching ownership markers.
limitations: Registry publication requires the PyPI package and OCI image to be publicly available.
The official MCP Registry is an external service with its own preview status and availability.

claims.claim: Provider output is constrained to a strict code proposal; trusted code supplies the target, provenance, fresh request identifiers, and active-policy binding before any execution.
limitations: The recipe uses deterministic fake or injected transports and does not contact a live Ollama service or establish model correctness, availability, privacy, or performance.
Provider version metadata is trusted configuration, not an attested response from the Ollama server.
A ready proposal remains untrusted data; this claim does not execute it or prove approval, mutation isolation, assertions, or end-to-end Harness behavior.

claims.claim: A provider-neutral controller retries only typed execution or assertion failures, rejects misbound executor results, and stops later calls at finite attempt, token, cooperative wall-time, proposal, diagnostic, and repeated-cycle gates; its runner incrementally enforces one shared command-output allowance across conditions and the action, terminates the child process group at observed excess, rolls back mutation, and preserves bounded source-bound terminal evidence.
limitations: Tests use deterministic fake providers or injected transports; no live model correctness, privacy, availability, performance, cost, or uplift claim is established.

The wall-time gate passes remaining deadlines to the Ollama and command-execution paths and stops later calls after an overrun; it cannot preempt a non-conforming provider or an in-process file write.
Prompt and completion tokens are provider-reported after a call; an over-reporting provider is rejected before execution or retry, but the controller cannot retroactively cap that call.

A child may write into the operating system's bounded pipe before the reader observes the first excess byte; the runner bounds userspace retention and terminates at observation, but this is not a strong resource-isolation boundary.
Controller state is not resumed across process restart and branch-and-select candidate evaluation is not implemented.
The controller does not add command mutation isolation; autonomous command retries remain gated by issue #27 and live runtime conformance.

claims.claim: A published profile proves isolation against host-secret reads, workspace escapes, resource exhaustion, and denied egress on supported hosts.
limitations: Not implemented and must not be credited as a current guarantee.

claims.claim: XT-Aegis achieves a specific rollback latency or token-cost reduction.
limitations: No numeric performance or token-savings claim is made until reproducible artifacts exist.
